core_domains.summary: EDX is an extension of the clinical examination. Start with history, symptom distribution, time course, examination and the clinical question before selecting and interpreting studies.
Organize EDX reasoning around motor neuron, root, plexus, peripheral nerve, sensory pathway, neuromuscular junction, muscle and relevant central nervous system processes.

Routine evaluation generally begins with NCS, followed by needle EMG. Motor studies commonly provide an early technical and physiologic map that helps guide subsequent sensory studies and needle examination.

Motor NCS evaluates CMAP latency, amplitude, area, duration and conduction velocity. Distal and proximal stimulation are needed to calculate segmental motor conduction velocity because distal latency includes distal nerve, NMJ and muscle components.

Sensory NCS evaluates SNAP latency, amplitude, duration and conduction velocity. Sensory responses are small and therefore particularly sensitive to technical factors and electrical noise. Onset latency represents the fastest conducting fibers; peak latency is useful when onset is difficult to mark but is not used to calculate conduction velocity.

Sensory studies may be antidromic or orthodromic. Antidromic recordings generally provide larger responses but can be followed by volume-conducted motor activity; orthodromic testing can help resolve uncertainty when a sensory response is absent or difficult to distinguish.

A lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion can preserve distal sensory responses because the sensory neuron cell body and distal axon remain connected to the recording site. This principle is important when distinguishing root-level disease from distal peripheral sensory neuropathy.

Axonal loss is commonly reflected by reduced CMAP and/or SNAP amplitudes. Needle EMG can show denervation and, with time, reinnervation changes. A single low amplitude should not be interpreted in isolation because technical factors, conduction block and other mechanisms can also reduce CMAP amplitude.

A primary demyelinating pattern is assessed using the overall combination of slowing, prolonged distal latencies, late-response abnormalities and conduction block or temporal dispersion, while avoiding overcalling abnormalities at common entrapment sites or from technical limitations.

Conduction block must be assessed with attention to CMAP amplitude and area, stimulation adequacy, segment length and temporal dispersion. Amplitude loss alone can be misleading; marked temporal dispersion can reduce amplitude without true conduction block, whereas substantial area loss is more specific.

F waves and H reflexes provide information about proximal motor or reflex pathways and complement routine distal studies. Their interpretation requires attention to nerve tested, stimulation, persistence, latency and the clinical context; absent late responses are not automatically abnormal when CMAP amplitudes are severely reduced.

Needle EMG should integrate insertional activity, spontaneous activity, MUAP morphology and activation/recruitment. Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves support active denervation but must be interpreted with timing and distribution. Fasciculations, myotonic discharges and other spontaneous patterns have different implications and require clinical correlation.

In acute axonal loss, reduced recruitment may precede mature MUAP remodeling. Chronic axonal loss is characterized by reinnervation with larger, longer-duration and often more complex MUAPs together with reduced recruitment. Timing of symptoms and denervation is essential.

Myopathy is evaluated by combining clinical pattern with NCS and needle EMG. Routine sensory responses are generally preserved unless there is another neuropathy; motor responses can be preserved or show reduced CMAP amplitude in severe or distal-predominant disease. Needle EMG may demonstrate small, short-duration, often polyphasic MUAPs with an early recruitment pattern, but the full pattern matters.

When neuromuscular transmission disease is suspected, routine NCS and needle EMG may be supplemented by repetitive nerve stimulation and exercise testing. Postsynaptic and presynaptic disorders produce different response patterns, but interpretation depends on protocol, muscle selection, baseline CMAP, temperature, medications and clinical phenotype.

Median neuropathy at the wrist is a localization diagnosis that must be separated from generalized neuropathy and other median lesions. Sensory abnormalities are often prominent. Comparative studies and segmental techniques can increase sensitivity, while clinical symptoms and examination determine whether an electrophysiologic median neuropathy represents clinically meaningful CTS.

Ulnar studies require localization using stimulation across relevant segments, sensory and motor responses, comparison with adjacent nerves when appropriate, and needle EMG of muscles supplied by different ulnar branches. Common entrapment sites should not be assumed to explain every abnormal result.

Radiculopathy is a clinical and electrodiagnostic localization problem. Sensory NCS may remain normal when the lesion is proximal to the DRG. Needle EMG distribution across muscles and, when appropriate, paraspinal sampling helps assess root involvement, but isolated abnormalities are insufficient for a confident conclusion.

Polyneuropathy assessment uses the distribution and symmetry of abnormalities, sensory versus motor predominance, axonal versus demyelinating features, length dependence and clinical time course. Incidental slowing at common entrapment sites can coexist with generalized neuropathy and should not automatically be equated with symptomatic entrapment neuropathy.

Motor neuron disorders may show widespread active and chronic denervation with reduced recruitment, while routine sensory studies can remain relatively preserved. Interpretation requires distribution across regions and correlation with upper and lower motor neuron clinical findings; conduction slowing from low CMAP amplitudes should not automatically be labeled demyelination.

Pediatric and ICU EDX require modified expectations because age, maturation, critical illness, edema, temperature, medications, cooperation and technical conditions can substantially influence results. Study selection and interpretation should account for the clinical setting.

Neuromuscular ultrasound complements EDX by providing structural and dynamic information about nerves, muscles and surrounding tissues. It does not replace physiologic EDX testing. Ultrasound findings should be interpreted with clinical history, examination and EDX results.

Technical quality is part of interpretation. Check limb temperature, electrode placement, stimulation intensity and location, distance measurement, artifacts, waveform morphology, co-stimulation and laboratory-specific reference values before labeling a result abnormal.

EDX is generally well tolerated but has potential risks and complications in selected patients. Operators should screen for relevant risks, use appropriate technique and follow local safety protocols.

chronic_demyelinating_polyneuropathy.book_concept: The textbook presents combined electrophysiologic criteria involving prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, prolonged late responses, and conduction block/temporal dispersion. The exact criteria must be applied with the laboratory's validated reference system and the relevant clinical context.
chronic_demyelinating_polyneuropathy.important_caution: Do not diagnose demyelination from one abnormal value, and do not apply generalized criteria across all disorders or technical situations.
